# Implement block: Mood Capsule Check-In (SwiftUI)

You are adding the "Mood Capsule Check-In" block from Native Cook to the user's iOS app. The block already exists as working SwiftUI code. Your job is to bring it into this project faithfully, not to write a new one that looks similar.

## The block

A mood check-in on a near-black screen (#0E0E10): under the grey question "How are you feeling?" sit five upright capsules (62 × 103 pt, 9.5 pt apart) in violet, blue, teal, yellow and orange, each with a pale mark in its middle, a glassy edge and a glow of its own colour; a dark tile with a gear and a chart icon is at the top right and a two-part control "Current mood / Overall today" at the bottom. A tap makes a capsule swell into a glowing lozenge (158 × 306 pt) in the middle of the screen that holds its mark, two translucent chips ("Emotions", "Context") and a round pale button with an up arrow, while the other moods turn into small grey capsules (42 × 73 pt) at its sides, the question blurs away, the mood's name ("Pleasant") appears above and the whole screen takes a haze of that colour. A sideways swipe, or a tap on a grey capsule, hands the lozenge to the neighbouring mood: one deflates as the other inflates, the name and the haze changing with it. A tap on a chip steps it through its words (it turns solid once it holds one), the round button shows a check and closes the lozenge, and a tap outside closes it without sending.

**Motion.** Two values lay out the row. `open` runs from 0 to 1 on a spring (stiffness 260, damping 20, mass 1, about 7% overshoot) and back on a stiffer-damped one (260 / 28); `focus` is the open mood's index and moves between moods on a spring (150 / 20). Each capsule's share of the lozenge is smoothstep(1 − |index − focus|); its width and height go from the resting size to small + (large − small)·share as `open` rises, so half way through a swipe two half-size blobs sit side by side, their edges softened by up to 3 pt of blur. The gap goes from 9.5 to 10 pt and the row is anchored on its middle at rest and on the focused capsule when open. A capsule's colour, glassy edge and 16 pt glow fade to a grey fill (white 10%) as it loses its share; the open one gets a 34 pt bloom at 62% and a haze of its colour over the screen (radial, 340 pt, 44% at the centre). Its mark moves 95 pt up and grows from 27 to 31 pt (17 pt in a grey capsule); the chips and the button scale with the capsule and come out of a 12 pt blur between a share of 0.5 and 1, fading in between 0.3 and 0.9. The question blurs by 8 pt and fades over the first half of `open`; the mood's name sharpens over its last 40% and cross-blurs during a swipe; the tile at the top fades and the selected segment takes 20% of the mood's colour with tinted text. A drag moves `focus` by one mood per 120 pt (30% of the pull past either end) and the release adds 0.15 s of the finger's speed, by one mood at most, with a selection haptic. A pressed capsule or button shrinks 6% in 120 ms; a chip dips to 90% and springs back (420 / 18) as its word changes; the button's arrow becomes a check in 280 ms and the lozenge closes 0.9 s after the tap, with a success haptic. "Overall today" slides the segment's thumb on a spring (300 / 26) and draws a 2 pt pale outline round the lozenge in 220 ms. The self-playing demo taps the fourth capsule at 0.8 s, swipes to the third at 2.0 s, back at 3.0 s, to the fifth at 4.0 s and back at 5.0 s, taps the first chip at 6.0 s and taps outside at 7.2 s, every 9 s, without haptics; a touch takes over and the loop starts again from the resting row 3 s later. Under reduced motion the row jumps to each new layout behind a 260 ms fade. The native ports keep the React Native timing code: its default-System reduced-motion veil jumps immediately, and the submit sequence still waits 901 ms. The automatic scope reset uses the same touch/reset path but suppresses its selection haptic so autoPlay remains silent. SwiftUI uses native system-font paragraphs and SF Symbols for the tile icons; Compose uses native system-font paragraphs and the source icon outlines. Compose uses a dim fallback for text/content blur below Android 12 and bounded Gaussian layers for capsule glow and soft edges on Android 26–27. Both native implementations guard empty mood lists and stale chip indexes.

## Reference source

The block is built and running in the Native Cook source repository. Each link below is a file on GitHub. To read one as plain text, replace `https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/` with `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/` in its address.

### Demo (start here)

- [MoodCapsuleCheckInDemo.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Forms/MoodCapsuleCheckIn/MoodCapsuleCheckInDemo.swift)

### Files of the block

- [MoodCapsuleCheckIn.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Forms/MoodCapsuleCheckIn/MoodCapsuleCheckIn.swift)

### Shared helpers the block uses

- [swift/NativeCook/Shared/ComponentSupport.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Shared/ComponentSupport.swift)

### Frameworks

It needs no framework beyond SwiftUI.

## Your instructions

_Anything specific to this app goes here: where the block should appear, what to rename, what to change. Left empty, integrate the block as it is._

## How to work

Work like an experienced iOS engineer joining an existing project: learn the app first, read only what you need, decide early how the block fits, then integrate it with as little disruption as possible. Take the steps in order.

**Done means** the block is reachable in the user's app and behaves like the reference in the iOS Simulator or on a device. A SwiftUI preview is useful while you work, but it is not the proof: build and run the app.

**Fidelity.** Bring over the real implementation. Keep its structure, colours, sizes, timings and curves. Change only what this project requires and what "Your instructions" ask for.

If you already learned this project earlier in the conversation, reuse what you know and skip step 2. Learn it again only if the project changed or something you need is missing.

### 1. Check where you are

- You need the project's files and a terminal. If this prompt was pasted into a chat that has neither, stop and say so: it has to be run by a coding agent opened on the project.
- Confirm the project is an iOS app built with Xcode (an `.xcodeproj`, an `.xcworkspace` or a Swift package with an app target). If it is something else, stop, say what you found, and do not create a new app inside it unless the instructions ask for one.

### 2. Learn the host app

- The app target, its deployment target and its Swift version.
- SwiftUI, UIKit or both, and how a screen is shown today: `NavigationStack`, a coordinator, a tab bar, a storyboard.
- How files join the target: a folder the project synchronises, or a file list in the project that you have to extend.
- Conventions: folder layout, naming, where colours, fonts and assets live.
- Type names the app already uses, so the block's types do not collide with them.

### 3. Read the block

- Swift files in a module do not import each other, so the demo alone will not lead you to the rest. The list above names every file of the block: read them all.
- The demo is how the source repository shows the block. Bring over what the demo shows, not the repository's gallery. Anything listed under "Used by the demo only" stays behind.
- Read the block's initialiser and its defaults. The demo may switch on an option that makes the block play by itself for a recording (for example `autoPlay`). Keep the option; leave it off in the user's app unless asked.

### 4. Decide the fit

- The source app targets iOS 17. If the host targets an older system, check each API the block uses and tell the user what would have to change before you lower anything. Do not raise the host's deployment target without asking.
- If a type or function name of the block already exists in the app, rename the block's one, in every file that uses it, and say that you did.
- Shared helpers: copy the ones the block uses next to it, or fold them into the block's files. Do not copy helpers it never calls.
- In a UIKit app, show the block through a `UIHostingController`.

### 5. Bring it in

- Add the block's files to the app target, keeping their names.
- Copy its asset catalogs, loose resources and fonts, and check that the names the code asks for match the names in the bundle: a wrong name compiles and then shows nothing.
- A `.metal` file has to be compiled into the same target as the code that calls its function.
- Keep reduced-motion handling, haptics and accessibility labels as they are in the source.
- Mount the block where the instructions say. With no instructions, add a screen named after the block and make it reachable the way the app's other screens are.

### 6. Run it

- Build the app target for a simulator with `xcodebuild` or the project's own script, and fix every error and new warning the block introduced.
- Run it and use the block: every state, every gesture, light and dark appearance if the block follows them, and once with Reduce Motion on.
- If the build or the simulator fails for a reason outside the block, report the error and ask how to continue.

### 7. Report

- Files added and changed, and anything renamed to avoid a collision.
- How to reach the block in the app.
- Anything that differs from the reference, and why.
